title: Strengths of Ionic and Covalent Bonds
lead: Every bond takes energy to break, and that energy measures its strength: the bond energy of a covalent bond and the lattice energy of an ionic solid. Average bond energies let us estimate the enthalpy change of a reaction, and the Born-Haber cycle finds a lattice energy from quantities that can be measured.
objectives: Describe the energetics of covalent and ionic bond formation and breakage
Use the Born-Haber cycle to compute lattice energies for ionic compounds
Use average covalent bond energies to estimate enthalpies of reaction
summary_html: The strength of a covalent bond is measured by its bond dissociation energy, that is, the amount of energy required to break that particular bond in a mole of molecules. Multiple bonds are stronger than single bonds between the same atoms. The enthalpy of a reaction can be estimated based on the energy input required to break bonds and the energy released when new bonds are formed. For ionic bonds, the lattice energy is the energy required to separate one mole of a compound into its gas phase ions. Lattice energy increases for ions with higher charges and shorter distances between ions. Lattice energies are often calculated using the Born-Haber cycle, a thermochemical cycle including all of the energetic steps involved in converting elements into an ionic compound.

Zinc oxide, ZnO, is a very effective sunscreen. How would the lattice energy of ZnO compare to that of NaCl?

answer.solution: ZnO would have the larger lattice energy because the Z values of both the cation and the anion in ZnO are greater, and the interionic distance of ZnO is smaller than that of NaCl.

exercises.prompt:
Which bond in each of the following pairs of bonds is the strongest?
(a) C–C or C=C
(b) C–N or C≡N
(c) C≡O or C=O
(d) H–F or H–Cl
(e) C–H or O–H
(f) C–N or C–O

answer.solution:
(a) C=C, 611 kJ/mol against 345 kJ/mol for C–C.
(b) C≡N, 891 kJ/mol against 290 kJ/mol for C–N.
(c) C≡O, 1080 kJ/mol against 741 kJ/mol for C=O.
(d) H–F, 569 kJ/mol against 432 kJ/mol for H–Cl.
(e) O–H, 464 kJ/mol against 415 kJ/mol for C–H.
(f) C–O, 350 kJ/mol against 290 kJ/mol for C–N.
In (a), (b) and (c) the two bonds join the same two atoms, and sharing more electron pairs makes the bond stronger, so a triple bond is stronger than a double bond, which is stronger than a single bond. In (d) the hydrogen bonds to two atoms of the same group, and bond strength decreases down the group, so H–F is stronger than H–Cl. Parts (e) and (f) join different pairs of atoms, so the values in Table 7.2 decide them.

exercises.prompt: How does the bond energy of HCl(g) differ from the standard enthalpy of formation of HCl(g)?

answer.solution: The bond energy of HCl(g), 432 kJ/mol, is the enthalpy change for breaking one mole of H–Cl bonds into gaseous atoms, $\text{HCl}(g)\longrightarrow \text{H}(g)+\text{Cl}(g)$, an endothermic change. The standard enthalpy of formation, $\kdHf=-92.307\;\text{kJ/mol}$, is the enthalpy change for making one mole of HCl(g) from its elements in their standard states, $\frac{1}{2}{\text{H}}_{2}(g)+\frac{1}{2}{\text{Cl}}_{2}(g)\longrightarrow \text{HCl}(g)$, an exothermic change. The two reactions differ in direction and in their starting materials: formation begins from H2 and Cl2 molecules, not from separate atoms, so it also includes breaking half a mole of H–H bonds and half a mole of Cl–Cl bonds. Adding those steps links the two values: $\kdHf\approx \frac{1}{2}(436)+\frac{1}{2}(243)-432=-92.5\;\text{kJ/mol}$, close to the measured value.

exercises.prompt: Using the standard enthalpy of formation data in Appendix G, show how the standard enthalpy of formation of HCl(g) can be used to determine the bond energy.

answer.solution: $$\begin{array}{ll}\text{HCl}(g)\longrightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_{2}(g)+\tfrac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_{2}(g) & \Delta H_{1}^{\circ}=-\Delta H_{\text{f}[\text{HCl}(g)]}^{\circ} \\ \tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_{2}(g)\longrightarrow \text{H}(g) & \Delta H_{2}^{\circ}=\Delta H_{\text{f}[\text{H}(g)]}^{\circ} \\ \tfrac{1}{2}\text{Cl}_{2}(g)\longrightarrow \text{Cl}(g) & \Delta H_{3}^{\circ}=\Delta H_{\text{f}[\text{Cl}(g)]}^{\circ} \\ \hline \text{HCl}(g)\longrightarrow \text{H}(g)+\text{Cl}(g) & \Delta H^{\circ}=\Delta H_{1}^{\circ}+\Delta H_{2}^{\circ}+\Delta H_{3}^{\circ}\end{array}$$$$\begin{array}{ll}D_{\text{HCl}}=\Delta H^{\circ} & =\Delta H_{\text{f}[\text{HCl}(g)]}^{\circ}+\Delta H_{\text{f}[\text{H}(g)]}^{\circ}+\Delta H_{\text{f}[\text{Cl}(g)]}^{\circ} \\ & =-(-92.307\;\text{kJ})+217.97\;\text{kJ}+121.3\;\text{kJ} \\ & =431.6\;\text{kJ}\end{array}$$

exercises.prompt:
Use principles of atomic structure to answer each of the following:1
(a) The radius of the Ca atom is 197 pm; the radius of the Ca2+ ion is 99 pm. Account for the difference.
(b) The lattice energy of CaO(s) is –3460 kJ/mol; the lattice energy of K2O is –2240 kJ/mol. Account for the difference.
(c) Given these ionization values, explain the difference between Ca and K with regard to their first and second ionization energies.
ElementFirst Ionization Energy (kJ/mol)Second Ionization Energy (kJ/mol)
K4193050
Ca5901140
(d) The first ionization energy of Mg is 738 kJ/mol and that of Al is 578 kJ/mol. Account for this difference.
1 This question is taken from the Chemistry Advanced Placement Examination and is used with the permission of the Educational Testing Service.

answer.solution: (a) When two electrons are removed from the valence shell, the Ca radius loses the outermost energy level and reverts to the lower n = 3 level, which is much smaller in radius. (b) The +2 charge on calcium pulls the oxygen much closer compared with K, thereby increasing the lattice energy relative to a less charged ion. (c) Removal of the 4s electron in Ca requires more energy than removal of the 4s electron in K because of the stronger attraction of the nucleus and the extra energy required to break the pairing of the electrons. The second ionization energy for K requires that an electron be removed from a lower energy level, where the attraction is much stronger from the nucleus for the electron. In addition, energy is required to unpair two electrons in a full orbital. For Ca, the second ionization potential requires removing only a lone electron in the exposed outer energy level. (d) In Al, the removed electron is relatively unprotected and unpaired in a p orbital. The higher energy for Mg mainly reflects the unpairing of the 2s electron.

exercises.prompt: The lattice energy of LiF is 1023 kJ/mol, and the Li–F distance is 200.8 pm. NaF crystallizes in the same structure as LiF but with a Na–F distance of 231 pm. Which of the following values most closely approximates the lattice energy of NaF: 510, 890, 1023, 1175, or 4090 kJ/mol? Explain your choice.

answer.solution: The lattice energy of NaF is closest to 890 kJ/mol. LiF and NaF have the same structure, so C is the same, and both contain ions with charges of 1+ and 1–, so Z<sup>+</sup> and Z<sup>–</sup> are the same. The only difference in $\kdHlat=\frac{\text{C}({\text{Z}}^{+})({\text{Z}}^{-})}{\kRo}$ is the interionic distance, and the lattice energy is inversely proportional to it. The longer Na–F distance therefore gives a smaller lattice energy than that of LiF: $$\kdHlat(\text{NaF})=1023\;\text{kJ/mol}\times \frac{200.8\;\text{pm}}{231\;\text{pm}}=889\;\text{kJ/mol}$$ Of the five values, 890 kJ/mol is the closest. The values 1023 kJ/mol and above would need a distance equal to or shorter than that in LiF, and 510 kJ/mol would need a distance about twice as long.

exercises.prompt:
For which of the following substances is the least energy required to convert one mole of the solid into separate ions?
(a) MgO
(b) SrO
(c) KF
(d) CsF
(e) MgF2

The reaction of a metal, M, with a halogen, X2, proceeds by an exothermic reaction as indicated by this equation: $\text{M}(s)+\text{X}_{2}(g)\longrightarrow \text{MX}_{2}(s)$. For each of the following, indicate which option will make the reaction more exothermic. Explain your answers.
(a) a large radius vs. a small radius for M+2
(b) a high ionization energy vs. a low ionization energy for M
(c) an increasing bond energy for the halogen
(d) a decreasing electron affinity for the halogen
(e) an increasing size of the anion formed by the halogen

answer.solution:
(a) A small radius for M2+. A smaller cation shortens $\kRo$, which raises the lattice energy, and $-\kdHlat$ is the step that releases energy.
(b) A low ionization energy for M. Ionization absorbs energy, so a smaller $\kIE$ adds less to $\kdHf$.
(c) An increasing bond energy for the halogen makes the reaction less exothermic, because breaking the X–X bond absorbs energy and $\kDbond$ adds directly to $\kdHf$; a decreasing bond energy makes it more exothermic.
(d) A decreasing electron affinity, meaning less energy released as each halogen atom gains an electron, makes $\kEA$ less negative and the reaction less exothermic; an increasing electron affinity makes it more exothermic.
(e) An increasing size of the anion makes the reaction less exothermic. A larger anion lengthens $\kRo$ and lowers the lattice energy, so less energy is released when the ions form the solid; a smaller anion makes it more exothermic.
Each answer follows from the Born-Haber cycle, $\kdHf=\kdHs+\kDbond+2\kIE+2\kEA-\kdHlat$ for MX2 (with $\kIE$ the sum of the first and second ionization energies), in which the endothermic steps raise $\kdHf$ and the exothermic steps lower it.

exercises.prompt: The lattice energy of LiF is 1023 kJ/mol, and the Li–F distance is 201 pm. MgO crystallizes in the same structure as LiF but with a Mg–O distance of 205 pm. Which of the following values most closely approximates the lattice energy of MgO: 256 kJ/mol, 512 kJ/mol, 1023 kJ/mol, 2046 kJ/mol, or 4008 kJ/mol? Explain your choice.

answer.solution: 4008 kJ/mol; both ions in MgO have twice the charge of the ions in LiF; the bond length is very similar and both have the same structure; a quadrupling of the energy is expected based on the equation for lattice energy

exercises.prompt:
Which compound in each of the following pairs has the larger lattice energy? Note: Mg2+ and Li+ have similar radii; O2– and F– have similar radii. Explain your choices.
(a) MgO or MgSe
(b) LiF or MgO
(c) Li2O or LiCl
(d) Li2Se or MgO

answer.solution:
(a) MgO. The charges are the same, 2+ and 2–, but O2– is smaller than Se2–, which lies further down group 16, so $\kRo$ is shorter in MgO.
(b) MgO. Li+ and Mg2+ have similar radii, as do F– and O2–, so $\kRo$ is about the same, but the product of the charges is (2)(2) = 4 for MgO against (1)(1) = 1 for LiF. The book gives 3900 kJ/mol for MgO and 1023 kJ/mol for LiF.
(c) Li2O. The product of the charges is (1)(2) = 2 against (1)(1) = 1 for LiCl, and O2–, similar in radius to F–, is smaller than Cl–, so both factors favor Li2O.
(d) MgO. The product of the charges is 4 against 2 for Li2Se, and with Mg2+ similar in size to Li+ and O2– smaller than Se2–, $\kRo$ is also shorter in MgO.
In each pair the lattice energy, $\kdHlat=\frac{\text{C}({\text{Z}}^{+})({\text{Z}}^{-})}{\kRo}$, is larger for the compound with the larger product of charges or the shorter interionic distance.

exercises.prompt:
Which of the following compounds requires the most energy to convert one mole of the solid into separate ions?
(a) MgO
(b) SrO
(c) KF
(d) CsF
(e) MgF2

answer.solution: (a) MgO requires the most energy. The energy to separate one mole of the solid into its gaseous ions is the lattice energy, $\kdHlat=\frac{\text{C}({\text{Z}}^{+})({\text{Z}}^{-})}{\kRo}$. MgO and SrO contain 2+ and 2– ions, so the product of the charges is 4; MgF<sub>2</sub> contains 2+ and 1– ions, a product of 2; KF and CsF contain 1+ and 1– ions, a product of 1. This places MgO and SrO above the other three. Between those two the charges are equal, so the smaller ion decides: Mg<sup>2+</sup> lies above Sr<sup>2+</sup> in group 2 and is smaller, which gives MgO the shorter $\kRo$ and the larger lattice energy, about 3900 kJ/mol.

The lattice energy of KF is 794 kJ/mol, and the interionic distance is 269 pm. The Na–F distance in NaF, which has the same structure as KF, is 231 pm. Which of the following values is the closest approximation of the lattice energy of NaF: 682 kJ/mol, 794 kJ/mol, 924 kJ/mol, 1588 kJ/mol, or 3175 kJ/mol? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: The lattice energy of NaF is closest to 924 kJ/mol. KF and NaF have the same structure, so C is the same, and both contain 1+ and 1– ions, so Z<sup>+</sup> and Z<sup>–</sup> are the same. The lattice energy, $\kdHlat=\frac{\text{C}({\text{Z}}^{+})({\text{Z}}^{-})}{\kRo}$, is then inversely proportional to the interionic distance, and the shorter Na–F distance gives a larger lattice energy than that of KF: $$\kdHlat(\text{NaF})=794\;\text{kJ/mol}\times \frac{269\;\text{pm}}{231\;\text{pm}}=925\;\text{kJ/mol}$$ Of the five values, 924 kJ/mol is the closest. A value of 682 kJ/mol would need a longer distance than in KF, and 1588 or 3175 kJ/mol would need a change in the ionic charges.
